title: SDK Standardization (Auth/Retry/Timeout/Streaming) — Customer Impact Brief (Hosted API)
content:
Audience
- PM + GTM + Support leadership for Hosted API (plus visibility for Eng/SRE/Security)

Purpose
We’re standardizing Redwood’s Python, TypeScript, and Go SDK behavior around authentication resolution, retries/backoff, timeouts, streaming semantics, and error taxonomy. This brief summarizes expected customer impact, rollout/comms plan, and how we’ll measure success.

Context / Problem statement (what customers experience today)
Across languages we have “it works in TS but not in Python” style issues, mostly clustering in:
- Inconsistent retry behavior for 429/5xx (including ignoring Retry-After in some cases)
- Timeout confusion (overall vs connect/read, and streaming timeouts not being honored)
- Streaming disconnects behind proxies and ambiguous guidance for safe retry
- Error objects missing request_id in some paths (hurts support + oncall triage)
- Auth environment variables and precedence differ per SDK (support friction; security review pressure)

Customer impact summary (what changes, who benefits, who might be surprised)
Primary positive outcomes
1) Fewer intermittent failures in production
- Better defaults for transient errors (429/5xx/network) with exponential backoff + jitter and respecting Retry-After.
- More predictable timeout behavior (consistent model and consistent mapping to underlying HTTP clients).

2) Faster support resolution and improved trust
- Typed errors consistently include request_id (and retry_count/timeout context where available), enabling Support/Oncall to correlate issues to gateway logs quickly.

3) Reduced “mysterious” streaming behavior
- Clear, consistent semantics for partial output, cancellation, and disconnect errors.
- Conservative guidance on when (and when not) to retry streaming to avoid duplicate side effects.

Potential negative / “surprise” impacts
A) Behavior changes that can look like regressions if customers were relying on old quirks
- Retries: some SDKs will retry less (or never) on certain classes of errors that were incorrectly retried (e.g., 4xx). This can reduce duplicate calls and billing concerns, but may surface failures that customers were masking via accidental retries.
- Timeouts: customers may see requests abort sooner if they previously relied on very long implicit defaults; conversely some might see fewer “hangs” due to better read/overall timeouts.

B) Slight changes in platform load characteristics
- Default retries increase resilience but can increase load during incidents if mis-tuned. SRE has asked for rollout monitoring + rollback triggers.

C) Streaming retry guidance remains conservative by design
- We will not “auto-resume” streaming in a way that risks duplicate generation or tool actions. Customers may request this, but our stance is to document safe patterns (idempotency keys, request_id logging, app-level dedupe).

Which customers are most impacted
- Enterprise customers behind corporate proxies/VPNs: will benefit from clearer streaming disconnect errors + recommended timeouts.
- Customers with strict latency budgets (interactive apps): will benefit from consistent timeouts and bounded retry attempts.
- Customers under bursty traffic/rate limits: will benefit from Retry-After compliance and better 429 backoff.
- Customers with compliance/security review: will benefit from consistent env var naming, precedence rules, and redaction-safe error messages.

Scope of standardization (customer-visible behaviors)
1) Authentication
- Single auth resolution order across SDKs (explicit client config wins; then environment variables; clear error when missing).
- Standard env var naming (with deprecations where applicable).
- Redaction requirements: secrets are never printed in exceptions or debug logs.

2) Retry policy (non-streaming)
- Retryable: 429, select 5xx, and network/transient transport errors.
- Not retryable: most 4xx (including 400) to prevent duplicate billing concerns and unintended side effects.
- Respect Retry-After where present (seconds or HTTP-date).
- Exponential backoff with jitter; cap on max delay; max attempts bounded.

3) Timeout model
- Standard model across SDKs with consistent naming and behavior. Document clear defaults and how to tune.
- Streaming uses a distinct set of timeouts/cancellation semantics (so it doesn’t “hang forever” and can be aborted reliably).

4) Error taxonomy
- Typed errors with common fields: message, status_code (if any), code (enum where available), request_id, retryable boolean, underlying cause.

5) Streaming semantics
- Consistent behavior for: cancellation, disconnect mid-stream, partial output visibility, and what error is thrown.
- Standard recommendation: do not blindly retry streaming; prefer idempotency patterns and logging request_id/attempt.

Rollout plan (high-level)
Guiding constraints
- Minimize breaking changes. Where customer behavior will change materially, provide:
  - migration notes
  - deprecation warnings (where feasible)
  - explicit configuration knobs to restore prior behavior (short term only)

Proposed rollout stages (8 weeks total target, with guardrails)
Stage 0 — Pre-announce (internal readiness)
- Confirm final standards/ADRs signed off by SRE + Security.
- Update docs drafts and support macros.
- Ensure platform gateway emits consistent Retry-After (429) and request_id across all paths.

Stage 1 — Beta releases (opt-in or labeled beta)
- Ship updated SDK versions with standardized behavior.
- Target: internal dogfooding + 3–5 design partners (mix of startup + enterprise).
- Capture early metrics (retry rate deltas, streaming disconnect rates, support signals).

Stage 2 — Stable releases (general availability)
- Publish stable versions for Python/TS/Go with consistent defaults.
- Publish migration guide and release notes.
- Coordinate comms across docs + changelog + announcement post.

Stage 3 — Adoption push + deprecation window
- Provide “upgrade assistant” docs: checklist + code snippets.
- Deprecate old env var names / legacy knobs with a clear timeline.

Rollback / stop-ship triggers (SRE-aligned)
- Sustained increase in platform load attributable to SDK retries (e.g., correlated retry storms during elevated 429s).
- Material increase in error rate or latency for top SDK methods after release (beyond expected variance).
- Spike in support tickets tagged “SDK retries/timeouts/streaming regression” post-release.

Customer communications strategy
Goals
- Set expectations: “more predictable and consistent behavior across languages” (not “we found major bugs”).
- Make upgrades feel safe: show defaults, explain why Retry-After matters, demonstrate how to tune without cargo-culting.
- Avoid alarming enterprise security teams: proactively mention redaction + env var guidance + auditability improvements.

Channels + messaging
1) Release notes (per SDK)
- Clear “What changed” bullets: auth precedence, retryable errors, timeouts, streaming disconnect error behavior.
- “How to keep previous behavior” section only if we must ship a compatibility knob (prefer not).

2) Docs update (single canonical page + per-language examples)
- One canonical “Retries and timeouts” doc with consistent examples for Python/TS/Go.
- A dedicated streaming reliability section with proxy guidance and recommended timeouts.

3) Migration guide
- Explicit mapping for renamed env vars/options.
- Callout: request_id is now included in all SDK errors; support will ask for it.

4) Customer success / sales enablement
- 1-pager for CSMs/SEs: “What’s new, why it matters, safe defaults, how to tune.”
- For customers concerned about duplicate billing: explain non-retryable 4xx stance + idempotency key guidance.

5) Support macro updates
- Standard questions: SDK name/version, request_id, retry_count, timeout settings, whether streaming is used, proxy/VPN.

Key success metrics (what we will measure)
Primary outcome metrics
1) Support ticket reduction (SDK inconsistency-related)
- Baseline: count tickets tagged retries/timeouts/streaming/auth mismatch across last 4–8 weeks.
- Target: 30–40% reduction in “SDK behavior mismatch / intermittent failures due to retry/timeout” within 6–8 weeks post-stable.
- Measurement: Zendesk/Jira tags + Support qualitative review.

2) SDK upgrade adoption
- Metric: % of active SDK requests coming from standardized versions (per language) within 30/60/90 days.
- Targets (initial):
  - 30 days: 25%+ of active traffic on new versions
  - 60 days: 50%+
  - 90 days: 70%+ (with enterprise lag expected; track separately)
- Note: If we can’t do telemetry in some environments, infer via User-Agent version parsing at gateway where available.

3) Retry behavior health
- Overall retry rate: should not spike materially under normal conditions.
- During 429/5xx events: retries should become more “well-shaped” (respect Retry-After, more spread due to jitter).
- Target: reduce “immediate retry” patterns on 429 (proxy for thundering herd) and reduce mean retry burstiness.

4) Timeout/streaming reliability
- Metric: streaming disconnect rate and distribution of disconnect reasons (where available).
- Target: reduction in “hung” streaming sessions and clearer error classification; aim for measurable decrease in enterprise proxy-related disconnect escalations.

Secondary metrics
- Time-to-triage for SDK-related incidents (Support/Oncall): should decrease due to request_id presence and consistent error fields.
- Customer satisfaction signal (CSM feedback, call notes): fewer “language mismatch” complaints.

Open questions / risks (PM callouts)
1) Backwards compatibility vs correctness
- If we discover customers rely on overly-aggressive retries, do we offer a temporary compatibility flag? Preference is “no” unless we have a top-account blocker.

2) Telemetry constraints
- Some customers disallow outbound telemetry. We should treat gateway-side version inference + standardized logging fields as the baseline.

3) Streaming expectations
- Customers may expect automatic resume. We should explicitly document why we don’t do this by default (idempotency + duplicate side effects) and provide recommended patterns.

4) Coordination dependencies
- Gateway must reliably emit Retry-After on 429 and request_id across all relevant error paths; otherwise SDK logic will be inconsistent no matter how good our client code is.

FAQ / positioning snippets (for PM/CSM/Support)
- “Is Redwood changing pricing or billing?”
  - No. This is client behavior standardization to reduce intermittent failures and prevent incorrect retries.
- “Will retries increase costs?”
  - Retries only trigger on transient failures; we cap attempts and respect Retry-After. Net effect should be fewer customer-visible errors without causing retry storms.
- “How do I debug a failure now?”
  - Use request_id from SDK error, include SDK version, and share retry_count/timeout settings. Support can trace request_id across gateway logs.

Next steps / owners
- Finalize customer-facing release notes template and migration guide outline (Wei Chen + Elliot Price; PM review by Henry Cho).
- Confirm rollout calendar + beta cohort (Monica Patel + Connor O’Brien; PM alignment).
- Align on success dashboards + alert thresholds during rollout (Allison Grant + SRE).
- Support enablement: update macros and internal runbook (Dev Patel + Owen Phillips).

Appendix: Notable customer signals informing this work
- Enterprise proxy streaming disconnects + need for explicit guidance (see SUP-29505).
- TS SDK retrying non-retryable errors creating duplicate billing concern (see SUP-29438).
- Go SDK ignoring Retry-After on 429 (see SUP-29477).
- Python streaming timeouts not honored (see SUP-29410).
- Support request to always include request_id in SDK errors (see INT-1182).
